idiom_name: class with a const identity member, hand-written operator== and std::hash by id
implementation_notes: C++ gives reference identity for pointers and references, but an entity class used as a value still needs its identity member and its comparisons written by hand: a const id member (ideally a typed id strong type), a non-member operator== comparing ids only, and a std::hash/std::equal_to specialization so unordered_map<CustomerId, ...> is keyed by identity. C++20's operator== = default is not a substitute - a defaulted equality compares subobjects member-wise, which is precisely the attribute equality an entity must avoid. When entities are shared as std::shared_ptr, the library already supplies reference/ownership identity: shared_ptr comparison compares the stored pointer, and std::owner_equal/std::owner_less compare ownership even for aliasing pointers, which is the right tool when different subobjects of one entity must be recognised as the same entity.
pitfalls: bool operator==(const Customer&) const = default; (or a defaulted operator<=>) compares every member, turning the entity back into an attribute value; default or write only id-based comparisons.

Comparing shared_ptr<Customer> with == compares the stored pointers, so two aliasing pointers to subobjects of the same entity compare unequal; use std::owner_equal / std::owner_less when ownership is the identity.

A const id member deletes assignment and move-assignment, so entity types are normally held by pointer or reference; decide this deliberately instead of letting callers discover a deleted copy assignment.
